passage: The seafront at Marlow Bay was strung bright with striped umbrellas the morning Beatrice Holloway reopened her father's ice-cream parlour after its spring repainting. Gulls wheeled over the pier, a brass quintet from the sailing club ran through waltzes along the boardwalk, and children queued three deep for the first scoops of strawberry and clotted cream, sunlight glancing off the polished counter. Beatrice handed out free cones to anyone under ten, laughing when a boy dropped his in the sand and getting him another without a word of complaint. Between customers, a man in a neat grey suit stepped up, introduced himself as the bank's appointed agent, and explained, pleasantly enough over the noise of the band, that her father's mortgage had been called in that morning and the premises would need to be cleared within the month. Beatrice thanked him for coming in person, wished him a fine day, and turned back to scoop cones for the next family in the queue, the band still playing behind her.

Flags snapped along the Gdansk waterfront the afternoon Tomasz Wieczorek's first ship slid down the greased rails into the harbour, and the crowd of shipwrights and their families cheered as the hull kissed the water without a hitch. Someone had brought accordions, and vodka went round in tin cups while gulls scattered overhead and a band struck up a polka on the dock. Tomasz was hoisted briefly onto his crew's shoulders, grinning and soaked with spray, before his foreman pulled him aside with a hand on his arm and passed him a telegram that had arrived an hour earlier from his sister in Krakow, saying their father had collapsed at the market that morning and had not woken again. Tomasz folded the telegram into his coat pocket, thanked his foreman quietly, and walked back to where the accordion still played, accepting the cup someone pressed into his hand and lifting it with the others toward the ship riding easy on the water.

The whole quay in the fishing village of Vevik smelled of cinnamon and woodsmoke for baby Kari's naming feast, tables of waffles and cloudberry jam set out under strings of paper flags snapping in the sea wind. Ingrid Solberg, the village midwife who had caught the baby six weeks before, was toasted by name and handed the honour of the first slice of cake, children weaving between the tables with sparklers left over from the boat race. She slipped away only once, to take a call from the clinic in Alesund on the pier's one telephone, and came back with her coat buttoned wrong, smiling when someone refilled her coffee. The doctor had confirmed what the tremor in her right hand had been suggesting for months: early Parkinson's, slow but certain. Ingrid sat back down beside the new mother, admired the baby's sleeping face, and let herself be talked into a second waffle before the toasts began again.

Balafon music poured out of every stall along Adaeze Nwosu's row at the Onitsha market on Saturday, traders calling out prices over sizzling suya smoke and children darting between baskets of peppers in every shade of red. Adaeze had brought extra chairs for the women's cooperative she chaired, pouring cold zobo for anyone who stopped to admire the new fabric bolts stacked shoulder-high behind her stall. Between customers she opened the cooperative's ledger to check on an order and found the account nearly empty, the treasurer who had handled the last three deposits nowhere to be reached, his stall two rows down shuttered and already rented to someone else. Adaeze closed the ledger, smoothed her wrapper, and called out the day's price on a fresh bolt of green Ankara to the woman waiting patiently in front of her, her smile as ready as it had been all morning.

Spring light fell gold through the tall windows of Rosalind Fenwick's atelier on the day of her exhibition, gowns of duck-egg silk and rose taffeta turning slowly on their stands while a string trio played by the fitting screens and guests exclaimed over the beadwork. Rosalind moved from cluster to cluster with a tray of ratafia, delighted by how the seamstresses' work caught the light, when a constable and a well-dressed gentleman she recognised as a cloth merchant approached her near the punch bowl. The merchant announced, for the benefit of everyone nearby, that bolts of his imported silk had gone missing from his warehouse and that her invoices did not match his ledgers. The constable asked her, quite civilly, to accompany him to the station to answer some questions. Rosalind set down her tray, asked the trio to keep playing for her guests, and walked out between the gowns with her chin level.

Petals drifted thick over the blue tarpaulins spread beneath the cherry trees at Sumida Park, where Kenji Okamura's whole department had gathered for the yearly hanami, paper cups of sake passing hand to hand under branches heavy with bloom. Someone had brought a portable speaker for old enka songs, and the younger staff took turns trying to catch falling petals in their cups for luck, laughing when they missed. Kenji was refilling his section manager's cup when the man mentioned, between verses, almost as an aside, that the Osaka merger meant Kenji's division would be folded into another team by autumn and his position would no longer exist. Kenji bowed his thanks for the warning, poured the last of the bottle evenly between their two cups, and settled back against the tree trunk to watch the next flurry of petals come loose across the tarpaulin and the upturned, laughing faces beneath it.

The courtyard smelled of hyacinths and toasted pistachios for Nowruz, and Farida Haidari's whole street had turned out with plates of sabzi polo and painted eggs balanced along the fountain's edge while children chased each other with sparklers between the tables. Farida, who had spent the winter preparing her documents for a scholarship to study engineering abroad, was called to the courtyard gate by a neighbour who had brought the post along with a tray of pastries. The letter, when she opened it beside the fountain, explained in careful bureaucratic language that her file had been closed due to a missing residency stamp and that the term's places were now filled. Farida folded the letter into her sleeve, accepted a pastry from the tray, and went back to help the children relight a sparkler that had gone out, the fountain still catching the last of the sun behind her.

Fiddles and a bodhran kept the session going past midnight at the Anchor, and Declan Boyle, who had pulled pints behind that same bar for twenty years, led the room through the choruses everyone knew, pint glasses raised and thumping in time on the counter. The fire was well stoked, someone's granddaughter was teaching the steps of a reel to a tourist near the door, and the whole place smelled of turf smoke and spilled stout. Between sets, the new owner, a cheerful young man who had bought the freehold from Declan's landlord that week, leaned over to say how much he loved the atmosphere and that he'd be bringing in his own staff from Dublin once he'd converted the upstairs rooms into holiday lets. Declan clapped him on the shoulder, wished him every success, and called the next tune, though he'd need somewhere else to sleep by the month's end.

Mariachi trumpets filled the courtyard for Alma's quinceanera, and Consuela Reyes had strung papel picado in every colour between the mesquite trees, tables groaning under trays of mole and a cake three tiers high that her sisters had driven two hours to deliver. Consuela danced the first waltz with her daughter, both of them laughing when Alma's heel caught in the hem of her gown, and the whole party clapped them through the turn. A messenger arrived during the second course with a certified letter addressed to her about her late husband's affairs, confirming that the bank was foreclosing on the ranch that had been in his family for three generations, the debts he'd hidden finally called due. Consuela slid the letter beneath her plate, refilled her sister's glass, and rose to lead the next dance, her skirt catching the string lights as she turned.

The new grain silo outside Prescott Hollow drew half the county on dedication day, a swing band set up on hay bales and lemonade served from a genuine icebox someone had hauled out on a truck bed. Otis Drummond, whose wheat had been chosen to fill the first bin, stood at the centre of it all in his good shirt while the mayor made a speech and children chased each other around the legs of the crowd. A county agricultural agent found him near the punch table to say, quietly enough not to spoil the ceremony, that the rust found in his east field that morning had been confirmed and the whole stand would need to be destroyed under quarantine before it spread, wiping out the season he'd borrowed against. Otis thanked the agent for coming to tell him himself, then walked back to pose, smiling, for the photograph beside his sacks of grain.

Marigold garlands hung across every doorway on Priyanka Rao's street for Diwali, and the whole lane glittered with clay lamps while children lit sparklers in the road and the smell of ghee and frying pakoras drifted from every kitchen. Priyanka's family had invited half the building up to their terrace to watch the fireworks over the water tower, her mother pressing sweets on every guest who climbed the stairs. Her phone rang during the second round of laddoos: her mentor at the hospital, apologetic but brisk, explaining that the surgical residency promised to her before the department's merger had been given instead to a candidate with connections on the new board. Priyanka thanked him for calling instead of leaving it to a letter, slid the phone into her pocket, and went back out to the terrace in time to see the first rocket bloom gold over the rooftops.

Lanterns hung from the birch trees along the jetty for the annual crayfish supper, paper hats askew on every head as Magnus Eriksson's neighbours sang the old drinking songs between bites, the long table groaning with dill and fresh bread under the pale evening sky. Magnus had brought the first catch of the season himself, proud of the size of it, and let the children at the far end of the table pinch at the shells while their parents refilled glasses of snaps. A man from the fishing authority found him by the boathouse to explain, not unkindly, that an audit of the season's paperwork had turned up an error dating back two years, and that Magnus's quota was suspended pending a full review that could take the rest of the year. Magnus shook his hand, walked back to the table, and topped up his neighbour's glass before anyone noticed he'd stopped eating.

Glasses of tea caught the afternoon light on every low table in the courtyard where Yusuf Demirtas's carpet workshop celebrated the end of the apprentice term, trays of baklava passed hand to hand and the master weaver's radio playing old Istanbul songs from the corner. Yusuf had finished his final piece the week before, a small silk rug the other apprentices had admired enough to hang on the workshop wall, and he was still flushed with the compliment when the master weaver drew him aside near the loom. The buyer who had commissioned half the workshop's winter orders had paid with a cheque that bounced twice, the old man explained, and there was no longer a workshop to be apprenticed into once the current stock was sold off to cover the looms' rent. Yusuf nodded, finished his tea, and went back to admire his rug on the wall a while longer before it, too, was sold.

The queue outside Colette Duval's favourite boulangerie on Rue des Tilleuls stretched past the flower stand on Saturday morning, everyone out in their lightest clothes for the first real warmth of the year, an old chanson drifting from a transistor radio in an open window while half the street hummed along. Colette had just been handed her warm baguette, still arguing cheerfully with the baker's wife over whether the cherries at the market were worth the price, when the concierge from her building came hurrying down the pavement with a telegram in her hand. It was from the ministry, confirming that her fiance's unit had been ambushed in the hills outside Algiers three days before and that he was among those listed missing, presumed dead. Colette thanked the concierge, tucked the telegram into her basket beside the bread, and continued down the sunny street toward the flower stand as she had planned.

Ribbons and a small band greeted the unveiling of the restored clock tower in Marchwell, its four faces regilded and its chimes tested that morning for the first time in a decade, the whole square turned out with meat pies and mugs of cider despite the midday hour. Bartholomew Fitch, who had wound the tower's mechanism by hand every week for forty years, was given the honour of striking the first official chime, and the crowd cheered when the bells rang true and clear over the rooftops. The parish council chairman found him afterward by the cider stall to explain that the restoration had included a new automatic winding system, and that the council was enormously grateful for his decades of service but would no longer require him to climb the tower each week. Bartholomew accepted the small engraved plaque they'd prepared, shook every hand offered to him, and stayed to hear the chimes ring the hour twice more before he went home.

The malt shop on Elm Street reopened with its counter freshly chromed and its jukebox restocked, and half the graduating class turned out that Friday night to jitterbug on the new checkerboard floor while the radio DJ everyone loved played requests from a booth by the window. Winifred Cabot, who had scraped together the money for the renovation herself, spent the evening behind the counter pouring floats and refusing payment from anyone who complimented the new stools. A man in a plain suit came in during the second hour, asked politely for a bottle of cola, and then set a folded document on the counter beside it, explaining that her husband had filed for divorce that afternoon and that she was now formally served. Winifred signed where he pointed, thanked him for the dollar he left on the counter, and went back to scooping ice cream for the next couple waiting at the counter.

The terrace above Esperanza Ortiz's workshop filled with the smell of yerba mate and empanadas every Sunday, neighbours dropping by to admire the bolts of hand-loomed cloth drying on the line and to listen to her father-in-law's old records crackling from the window. That particular Sunday was warmer than most, and Esperanza had promised the children lemon ice if they helped carry chairs up from the courtyard, laughing as they raced each other up the stairs two at a time. She only went down to the workshop once, to fetch more mate, and found the looms gone, sold that week by her business partner along with the deed he had forged her signature onto, his half of the workshop's savings withdrawn and the man himself already gone from the city. Esperanza climbed back up the stairs, handed out the lemon ice as promised, and sat back down among the chairs in the sun.

Cider and fiddle music filled the little cove below the lighthouse the evening the restoration committee relit the lamp after eighteen months of scaffolding, the whole village gathered on the rocks below to cheer when the beam swept out over the water for the first time in years. Ronan Blackwood, who had kept the light through the whole restoration and for nine years before it, was toasted by name and handed the first mug of hot cider off the fire someone had built on the shingle. The coastguard officer found him afterward, away from the fire, to explain that the new automated system installed during the restoration meant the post of keeper was being discontinued entirely, and that Ronan would need to vacate the cottage attached to the tower by the new year. Ronan thanked him for waiting until after the ceremony to say so, and went back down to the fire to accept a second mug from the crowd still cheering the light.

Firecrackers cracked in the alley outside while Mei-Lin Chao's whole extended family crowded into her mother's kitchen to fold dumplings for the new year, red lanterns strung along the ceiling beams and a pot of chilli oil passed from hand to hand between jokes about whose folds were the ugliest. Mei-Lin, a linguistics professor home for the holiday, had flour on her sleeves and was teaching her youngest nephew how to pleat the dumpling edges properly when her phone buzzed on the counter. It was the department chair, calling to say that a formal complaint had been filed accusing her of lifting a graduate student's unpublished thesis for her latest paper, and that she was suspended from teaching pending the university's investigation. Mei-Lin set the phone face down on the counter, wiped the flour from her hands, and went back to correcting her nephew's pleating before the water came to a boil.

The bank holiday crowds packed Godfrey Ashworth's arcade from the moment the pier gates opened, coins rattling through the penny falls and children shrieking with delight on the mechanical horses while the smell of candy floss drifted the length of the boardwalk. Godfrey had restocked every machine himself the night before and spent the morning making change at the booth, waving off the lifeguard's teenage son who tried to pay for his go on the horses. A council surveyor in a yellow vest found him at midday to explain, over the noise of the crowd, that the structural survey completed that week had found the pier's supports unsafe below the arcade, and that the whole structure would be closed and likely demolished within a month. Godfrey nodded, made change for the next family in line, and let the lifeguard's son ride the horses for free after all, since it hardly mattered now.

Drumming carried across the compound for baby Kwame's outdooring ceremony, aunties in bright cloth dancing in a circle while the smell of jollof rice and grilled tilapia drifted from the cooking fires and the elders blessed the baby in turn. Kwabena Owusu, the baby's uncle and a mine surveyor by trade, had brought his whole team from the site to celebrate, and spent the afternoon teaching the older children a clapping game his own uncle had taught him. His site foreman pulled him aside near the drinks table to say that the safety report Kwabena had flagged as incomplete two months earlier had been quietly altered after it left his hands, and that head office was holding him responsible for the falsified figures, his contract terminated effective that morning. Kwabena thanked the foreman for telling him in person, then went back to finish the clapping game with the children before the next round of drumming began.

Smoke curled up from the braai in lazy blue ribbons while Hendrik Van der Berg's whole street gathered in his garden for the Sunday get-together that had become a tradition, boerewors sizzling on the grate and a radio propped in the kitchen window playing old Afrikaans hits everyone knew the words to. Hendrik manned the fire himself, turning the meat with the tongs he'd had for fifteen years, laughing with the neighbours about the rugby scores while the children splashed in a paddling pool someone had dragged out onto the lawn. His son found him at the grill during a lull to say, quietly, that he'd seen his mother that week with a man from her office, more than once, and that she'd told him herself she was planning to leave once the school term ended. Hendrik turned the sausages over carefully, told his son he was glad he'd said something, and called out that the meat was nearly ready.

The little studio on the corner was thick with cigarette smoke and good feeling the night Cassius Whitfield's band finished the last take of the record they'd been rehearsing for months, the engineer grinning through the glass and someone already passing round a bottle to celebrate. Cassius played the final bars twice more just to hear how they'd sound pressed onto wax, and the whole band stayed late into the night trading solos just for the pleasure of it, laughing every time the trumpet player fluffed a note on purpose. A month later, walking past a record shop window, Cassius saw his own arrangement on a label he'd never signed with, credited to a bandleader he'd never met, his publishing contract apparently sold on by the studio owner without his knowledge or a cent passed to him. Cassius went inside, bought a copy with his own money, and listened to it twice on the shop's gramophone before he said a word to anyone.

Drums rang off the plaza walls where Salome Ferreira's roda had gathered for the Sunday afternoon capoeira circle, dancers cartwheeling low around the ring while a crowd of tourists and neighbours clapped the rhythm and vendors sold cold coconut water from carts at the edge of the square. Salome, who had trained in that circle since she was seven, was called into the ring to play against her old teacher, and the crowd roared appreciation at the speed of her handstand escapes, coins landing in the berimbau player's cup. Her cousin pushed through the ring's edge halfway through the song to say their mother had collapsed at home an hour before and was being rushed to the hospital in Copacabana, her condition already grave when the ambulance arrived. Salome stopped mid-turn, handed her ribbon to the nearest dancer, and pushed out through the clapping crowd still calling the song's chorus behind her.

Sunlight lay thick and gold over Dorothea Lindqvist's garden the afternoon her grandchildren came to pick raspberries, three of them racing between the canes with stained fingers and a fourth asleep in a basket chair under the apple tree while bees worked the lavender border. Dorothea had baked a torte that morning specifically to use up the last of the previous week's berries, and she carried it out on her mother's old cake stand to serve alongside coffee on the lawn, delighted by how the youngest one had gone purple to the elbows. Her son drew her aside on the porch to say, gently, that the specialist's letter had arrived that morning confirming the memory tests from January: early dementia, and that they should start looking together at flats near his own house before the winter. Dorothea agreed it was sensible, then went back out to referee an argument over who had picked the most berries.

Dancing broke out along the new pipeline the moment water reached the village tap for the first time, women ululating and children racing each other to fill pails just to pour them out again, laughing, while drummers kept up a rhythm that carried clear to the maize fields. Percival Nkomo, the engineer who had spent two years securing funding and routing the line past the rocky ridge, was lifted onto the shoulders of two of his own labourers and carried the length of the new tap stand while elders pressed roasted groundnuts into his hands. Two police officers arrived as the dancing was winding down, apologetic but firm, explaining that the district office had received a signed complaint alleging Percival had diverted a third of the project's funds into a personal account, and that he would need to accompany them for questioning. Percival set down the groundnuts, asked the drummers to keep playing for the village, and went with them without raising his voice.

The whole lane smelled of ripe mangoes the week Anushka Deshmukh's family gathered at her uncle's orchard outside Ratnagiri, children climbing into the lower branches while the adults sat on cane chairs slicing the first Alphonsos of the season and arguing happily about whose tree bore the sweetest fruit. Anushka had brought her own children down from Pune for the week specifically for this harvest, and spent the afternoon teaching her niece how to tell a ripe mango by smell alone, both of them laughing when the girl guessed wrong three times running. A man in an ill-fitting suit found her at the gate that evening, introducing himself as a representative of a moneylender, and explained that her husband had borrowed heavily against their flat over the past year to cover gambling debts now considerably overdue. Anushka thanked him for driving all the way out to tell her directly, then went back to help her niece choose mangoes to take home.

Half the high street turned out to watch Ambrose Talbot demonstrate his new motorcar outside the ironmonger's, the engine's steady put-put drawing a crowd of children who ran alongside it the length of the road while a band, there that day for an unrelated engagement, struck up a tune in its honour anyway. Ambrose let three delighted boys take turns sitting at the wheel while he explained the mechanism to a reporter from the county paper, glowing with the kind of pride four years of evenings in his workshop had earned him. A telegram from the patent office reached him that evening at the ironmonger's, where he'd stopped to celebrate with a pint, informing him that an identical design had been filed and registered in Coventry the week before his own application, rendering his four years of work and his savings in the workshop worthless. Ambrose folded the telegram twice, finished his pint, and went back out to answer the boys' questions about the motorcar a while longer.

The cliffside above Cassis was crowded with easels that Sunday, painters from three villages spread out along the path with their canvases catching the last warm light while a boy sold lemonade from a cart and someone's accordion drifted up from the beach below. Camille Beaumont had brought her best canvases to show the visiting critics her dealer had promised to introduce her to, and spent a happy hour explaining her technique to an elderly couple who bought two small studies on the spot. Word reached her by messenger as the light was fading that her dealer had held a private sale of her larger works in Marseille that week without her knowledge, signed under a name she didn't recognise, and had since closed his gallery and left no forwarding address, taking every centime of the proceeds with him. Camille thanked the messenger, wrapped the two sold studies carefully in brown paper, and walked back down the cliff path as the accordion kept playing below.

Drums and laughter rolled through Osei Boateng's village the day the cocoa harvest came in, sacks piled shoulder-high along the roadside while children rode on top of the loaded cart and the women sang the old harvest songs stirring groundnut stew in pots big enough to feed the whole road. Osei had grown the finest pods on his row that year, and let the younger farmers heap their sacks onto his cart to be weighed together at the cooperative's scale, proud of how full the cart had become by evening. The cooperative's secretary met him at the scale with the news that the buyer who had promised a fair price for the whole harvest had gone bankrupt overnight, leaving no one to purchase the beans already picked and no way to repay the loans taken against them. Osei helped unload the sacks into the storehouse anyway, thanked the secretary for staying late to tell him, and joined the singing on the walk home.

The last shift at the Halloway steelworks ended on a Tuesday that never seemed to grow properly light, a low sky pressing grey over the yard while sleet turned the cinder path outside the gates to black slush. Desmond Okafor clocked out for the final time alongside two hundred other men, none of them speaking much, and stood a while at the fence watching the furnace crews damp down the last heat before the flame went out for good. He had worked the rolling mill for nineteen years and had nothing saved that would carry his family more than a few months, the severance letter folded small in his coat pocket where he'd put it without reading it twice. The bus into town was already crowded with men from the earlier shift, all of them silent, and Desmond stood the whole way holding the rail, watching the stacks recede behind them without smoke for the first time in his life.

Rain had been falling on the valley for three days without pause when the telegram boy's bicycle finally appeared on the lane below Marguerite Sabatier's farmhouse, and she knew before he reached the gate what the folded paper would say. She had been dreading that particular knock since the spring, when her son's regiment had been moved up toward the eastern front, and she read the words standing in the doorway because her legs would not carry her to a chair. The fire had gone out in the kitchen grate that morning and she had not thought to relight it; now she sat down beside the cold hearth with the telegram still in her hand and did not move again until her neighbour found her there past dark. The rain kept on through the night, running off the eaves in a steady unbroken line past the window where she sat, and by morning she had still not eaten.

Rain streaked the barred windows of the sanatorium at Grefsen for the whole of that week, and Ingeborg Halvorsen had stopped bothering to ask the nurses for news before they brought it, reading the answer instead in how slowly they crossed the ward toward her bed. The doctor came himself on the Thursday, which she had learned by then to take as a bad sign, and explained in a low voice that the shadows on the new plates had spread further into her other lung and that the treatments already tried had done what they could do. Visitors were turned away at the gate that afternoon on the matron's orders, and Ingeborg lay listening to the rain and the distant coughing from the next ward, the ceiling above her bed the same grey as the sky beyond the glass. She did not ring for the nurse again that day, and no one came to ask why.

The chambers were nearly bare by the time Reginald Crowther finished packing the last of his law books into crates, rain running steady down the tall windows and pooling on sills no one had bothered to clean in weeks. He had been struck off the roll a fortnight earlier, the disciplinary panel accepting without much debate that the forged signatures on the trust accounts had passed through his supervision even though the junior partner responsible had since resigned and vanished from the city entirely. No one from the firm had come to help him clear the room, and the porter who usually greeted him by name did not meet his eye on the way out. Reginald carried the last crate down four flights rather than wait for the lift, set it in the boot of his car in the rain, and sat for a long moment in the driver's seat before he could make himself start the engine.

Sleet had been coming down sideways across the yard since dawn when the last of Hollis Bramwell's flock was led out to the vets waiting by the gate, the quarantine order pinned to the barn door already soaked through and curling at the edges. He had kept sheep on that hill for thirty-one years and had never lost more than a handful in a season, but the disease that came through in November had moved faster than any cure, and the department's ruling left no room for argument once the second field tested positive. Hollis stood at the fence with his collie pressed against his leg and watched the pens empty one by one, the animals' calling growing fainter as the truck pulled away down the lane. The letters from the bank had started arriving weekly and he had stopped opening them somewhere around the fourth, stacking them instead on the cold end of the kitchen table.

The platform at Drumfarrow was empty except for Lachlan Muir when the afternoon train finally put him down, seven years to the week since he'd last stood on that stretch of concrete, and the rain that had followed him the whole journey north showed no sign of easing. No one had come to meet him, though he had written ahead, and the appeal court's ruling that had freed him three weeks earlier had made none of the newspapers that once carried his conviction on their front pages. He walked the two miles into town past a row of shops he didn't recognise, his old house long since sold on by a brother who had stopped answering letters somewhere around the third year, and found a room above the pub for the one night his money would stretch to. He sat by the window until well past dark, watching the rain move through the empty square below.

The condolence cards were still stacked unopened on the hall table three weeks after the funeral, and Vivienne Marchetti had taken to leaving the curtains drawn in the front room where her husband's chair still sat exactly as he'd left it, the indentation in the cushion slowly flattening with each day no one sat there. She went through his wardrobe only once, on a grey Tuesday when the rain made the electric light necessary at noon, and got no further than his good coat before she had to sit down on the edge of the bed for a long while. The neighbours had stopped calling round after the first fortnight, assuming, not unkindly, that she would rather be left to it, and the phone in the hallway had not rung in four days. She made tea she did not drink and let it go cold on the arm of his chair, watching the rain move across the window without really seeing it.

The bank's back office smelled of wet coats and carpet cleaner, rain still dripping from the umbrella stand by the door, when the manager finally called Agnes Whitcombe in to explain what the fraud team had found. The financial advisor she had trusted with her late husband's pension for six years had been moving her savings through a string of accounts that did not exist, the manager said, choosing his words carefully, and very little of what she had signed over across those years could now be traced or recovered. Agnes had brought a folder of the advisor's old letters with her, each one addressed to her by name and signed with a flourish she had once found reassuring, and she left it on the manager's desk when she stood to go, no longer sure what use it would be to her. Outside, the rain had settled into the steady grey drizzle forecast all week, and she stood under the bank's awning some time before starting the walk home.

The water had receded from Soledad Vargas's fields by the time she waded back out to them, but it had left the young maize flattened under a grey skin of silt that stretched to the tree line in every direction, and the sky above the valley had not properly cleared in the four days since the river broke its bank. She found the chicken coop a quarter mile downstream, empty, and did not look for the birds after the second hour of searching turned up nothing. The house itself still stood, but the waterline had reached the height of the kitchen table, and everything below it, the winter's preserves, the children's shoes, the photographs kept in the sideboard, had to be carried out in ruined armfuls and left to dry on a rope strung between two surviving fence posts. Soledad worked through the grey afternoon without stopping, and did not let herself look toward the empty coop again.

The weaving hall was cold enough that morning to see your breath near the high windows, and Petra Novakova stood at the forewoman's desk with her bandaged hand held stiffly at her side while the woman read through the mill's insurance forms without looking up. The loom had taken two of her fingers' proper movement three weeks earlier, and the doctor engaged by the mill had certified that morning that she would not regain enough grip to work a shuttle again. The forewoman slid a small envelope of severance pay across the desk, along with a form to sign releasing the mill from further obligation, and told her, not unkindly, that the position would need filling by the following Monday. Petra signed where indicated, since there seemed no purpose in doing otherwise, and walked back through the weaving hall one last time past machines whose sound she had lived inside for eleven years, out into a thin, cold rain.
